I built it alone for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, Oct 27 to Nov 4, 2026, with Claude Code as a coding assistant. A street photo of a flood in Metro Manila gets a depth reading in MMDA's flood-gauge levels, or an honest "can't tell" when no car wheel or adult in it is clear enough to read. Faces are blurred on Lusot's own server before Meta's models see the photo. SAM 3.1 outlines the water, wheels and people, Muse Spark describes where the water meets them, and published code, not the models, picks one of nine levels. Every figure comes from a small sample, and the project calls its results indicative. None of 15 flood-free, open-license street photos was reported as flooded. On the sealed test, scored once on Nov 3, 2026 with the system frozen, it gave a reading for 1 of 6 photos and refused the other five, and that one reading was deeper than its label. The 5,900+ is 5,986 tests passing in CI on Nov 10, 2026. Lusot is not affiliated with MMDA, and a reading is not advice to cross.

`SAM 3.1` `Muse Spark` `Python` `TypeScript` `React` `AWS` `OpenCV` `Node.js` `Leaflet`<br>The live system was shut down on Nov 10, 2026; the demo replays saved real samples, and everything else in it is simulated. [Live demo](https://lusot.vercel.app) · [Repository](https://github.com/RVBCosme/Lusot-submission)

Thesis team lead, then sole developer of the rebuild; Kotlin, Python, Flask and MySQL; dlib's 68 facial landmarks and OpenCV; 2025, and October to November 2026.">
</picture>

I led our thesis team in 2025, and a teammate updated the app in mid-2026. From October 2026 I rebuilt it alone, directing an AI coding agent, and measured it. A Kotlin app on an Android phone sends camera frames over the driver's own network to a Python and Flask server, which finds the face with dlib's 68 facial landmarks and OpenCV and measures how open the eyes and mouth are and where the head points. A time rule decides what counts, the app speaks the alert, and when it can't see the face it says so instead of guessing. I tested it once on people it had never seen: it met 0 of its 15 accuracy targets, and the project site says so. The 713 ms is the 95th percentile from camera capture to result, on one phone at a desk on Nov 11, 2026; it rose to 887 ms with the server PC heavily loaded. The 26 of 30 is an idealized episode count from that sealed final test, and the same count missed 22 yawn episodes. It's an academic prototype, not a safety device.

`Kotlin` `Android` `Python` `Flask` `OpenCV` `dlib` `NumPy` `MySQL`<br>Private repository, walkthrough on request. [Project site](https://eyedtrack.vercel.app)

  <img src="assets/profile/light/ratchet.svg" width="100%" alt="Sheet 4 of 6, detail C, AI systems, with an illustrated run that moves through five phases, Spec, Red, Green, Review and Memory, while the hook blocks one call outside its phase and every step is added to a chained ledger that a verify script checks line by line: RATCHET, a gated pipeline for IBM Bob, an AI coding agent. Top 50: one of the 50 top-scoring qualified submissions, with no rank given; 8 of 8 hidden referee tests passed by the gated run, one run with one seed, an illustration, not a benchmark; 52 ledger records verified, tamper-evident, not tamper-proof. Sole developer; IBM TechXchange 2026 Pre-conference Dev Day Hackathon; Python, pytest and bandit; August 2026.">
</picture>

I designed and built it alone over the two days of the IBM TechXchange 2026 Pre-conference Dev Day Hackathon, Aug 29 to 30, 2026. AI agents made writing code almost free, so the slow part became trusting it. RATCHET makes IBM Bob, an AI coding agent, work in five phases: Spec, Red (write a failing test), Green (the smallest change that makes it pass), Review and Memory. A hook that runs before every tool call blocks anything outside the current phase, and a person opens each gate with one command. Hooks, never the model, write every step to a ledger in which each line carries a keyed hash linking it to the line before, and a verify script checks the chain and names the first line that doesn't match. Top 50 means one of the 50 top-scoring qualified submissions, from the organizers' email of Sep 29, 2026, which gives no rank. The gated run passed 8 of 8 hidden referee tests, but that is one run with one seed: an illustration, not a benchmark. The verify script checked 52 ledger records; the ledger is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof against someone with a shell.

`Python` `IBM Bob` `TDD` `pytest` `bandit` `watsonx.ai Granite`<br>The repository reports both demo runs, gated and unguarded. [Repository](https://github.com/RVBCosme/Bob-Passing)

Sole developer; React, Express, SQLite; in use since September 2026, with online ordering in progress; May 2026 to now.">
</picture>

I started it while working as the Council's assistant office manager, to automate the paperwork I was handling. It covers the Council's stock, Official Receipts, cash and check vouchers, petty cash, members, annual dues and officers, and runs on a single office PC. Officers can reach it from their phones over the office WiFi, and nothing goes to the cloud. Every peso and centavo is exact, and a checked backup is made within about two minutes of any change. Built test-first, with every screen checked at nine widths in two browser engines, 1,000+ layout checks in all. It has been in use since September 2026, and I'm adding online ordering. The 4,000+ is 4,170 checks, all passing, on Sep 12, 2026, and the layout checks were 1,092 at the release of Sep 24, 2026; both have grown since. The documentation counts the screens two ways, so I round down to 20+.

`TypeScript` `React` `Vite` `Tailwind` `Express` `SQLite` `Zod` `Vitest` `Playwright`<br>Private repository, walkthrough on request. I also built the Council's new public website, in Laravel and Filament; it isn't live yet, and its online shop is in progress.
